To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the lungs of the fetal lamb and rabbit have a large volume of fluid, that the fluid is rich in chloride but almost free of protein, and that the fluid is rapidly reabsorbed into the pulmonary microcirculatory bed at birth.

liquid is removed from the lungs by the pulmonary vascular bed, not by lymphatics, that removal of liquid is initiated even before birth, and that removal of liquid occurs by a combination of mechanisms that are not fully understood.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics of liquid in the fetal lungs and with mechanisms that regulate the flow of liquid across the pulmonary epithelial barrier before and after birth.
the mechanisms by which the lungs of the fetus and newborn are able to rapidly adapt to the demands of gas exchange at birth.
elucidation of the mechanisms that control pulmonary liquid flow in the fetus and the newborn.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
pulmonary liquid dynamics are complex, but that they are not difficult to understand.
the lungs of the fetus and newborn contain liquid that is rich in chloride and almost free of proteins, and that this liquid is removed by a combination of active and passive mechanisms.
the dynamics of pulmonary water before birth and during the transition from fetal to neonatal life is a complex process involving a variety of interacting factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lungs of the fetus are designed to produce liquid, and the lungs of the newborn are designed to absorb liquid.

the dynamics of pulmonary liquid before and after birth are a function of the interplay between transvascular pressure, transvascular protein osmotic pressure, and transvascular hydrostatic pressure gradients.
the lungs of newborn mammals are prepared for gas exchange at birth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lungs of newborns and infants are not just passive structures, but rather are active participants in the process of gas exchange.
